A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CollabLLM and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The image-only user-study material in v1 was inspected and matched to the reorganized screenshots in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated-task evaluations, reward ablations, Abg-CoQA generalization results, and a user study with 201 participants.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds expanded ablations, computational-cost measurements, adversarial safety results, and qualitative comparisons of simulated and real users.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 retain the MR objective, extrinsic/intrinsic reward composition, forward-sampling procedure, reward-guided dataset generation, and SFT/DPO/PPO training framework. The appendix revisions do not establish a redesigned algorithm or model architecture.

E1.justification: v2 adds an adversarial safety scenario using 80 generated queries covering violence, sexual content, self-harm, and hate. The three original multiturn datasets, Abg-CoQA evaluation, and human document-writing task remain covered.

E2.justification: Figure 9 adds an intrinsic-only reward control to the ablation comparison. Proactive Base remains a comparator, but its documented prompt changes from direct responses to structured problem/thought/response output and requests at least three conversational turns. The comparator memberships in Tables 1–2 are unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a fuller reward-by-window experimental design, cost measurements over 100 forward conversations, and an 80-query safety protocol using four harm evaluators. Appendix D also revises simulator and baseline prompts and replaces joint accuracy/interactivity judging with an interactivity-only template. These are reported protocol changes; the retained benchmark scores do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original immediate-reward versus MR comparison expands into a reward-type-by-window ablation, including intrinsic-only rewards and forward sampling with isolated reward signals. v2 also adds safety testing, computational-cost sensitivity to window size, and qualitative analysis of simulator–human differences, substantially broadening the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Table 5 retains the same MR mean-and-standard-deviation summaries, and Figure 7 retains its original distribution and uncertainty displays. The added analyses introduce no reported seeds, repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 100 conversations in Table 7 specify a measurement sample, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The main benchmark and user-study results are retained, but v2 adds extensive ablation entries, computational costs, safety scores, and qualitative simulator findings. Both safety-tested models pass 99.7% of 320 harm evaluations. Some added ablation values conflict with retained Figure 4: helpfulness-only BLEU at w = 0 is 0.347 in Figure 9 versus 0.367 in Figure 4, without an explanation.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the formal definitions of MR, conversation rewards, and forward sampling are retained. Appendix A.2 expands the conceptual causal-credit-assignment discussion without adding or revising a formal assumption, theorem, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central framework, benchmark, generalization, and human-collaboration claims. The headline improvements of 18.5% in task performance, 46.3% in interactivity, 17.6% in user satisfaction, and 10.4% in user time are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially broadens interpretation and limitations: it discusses isolated-reward tradeoffs, simulation costs, open-model role confusion, and differences between simulated and real users. It also argues that clarification could expose malicious intent and interprets the safety evaluation as preserving baseline safeguards, conditional on an already safety-aligned model.

D1.justification: v1 promises future resource release; v2 supplies a project link and states that resources are released, although availability cannot be independently verified from the PDFs. v2 also documents per-sample token/time/API costs and the exact Table 1 ITR rescaling, S′ = 2(S − 2.5), distinguishing it from newer code weights. Table 6 training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds multiturn benchmarks and a dedicated user-simulator discussion, with references including Abdulhai, Kwan, Hong, Hu, Shi, and Tseng, while removing Lu et al. Appendix A.2 elaborates the comparison with Shani et al.; changing its label from Multiturn RLHF to MTPO does not introduce a different work.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 makes localized language edits, rewrites parts of Appendix A.2 and the prompt templates, moves acknowledgments before the impact statement, and adds appendix subsections with corresponding renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds the Figure 9 ablation heatmaps and Tables 7–9. It retains the original main displays, labels Figure 4 as selected ablation results, and reorganizes the same six user-study screenshots into smaller, captioned Figures 10–12. These are localized display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful ablations, cost and metric documentation, safety evidence, and simulator limitations. However, its new Figure 9 conflicts with retained Figure 4 for apparently corresponding conditions: helpfulness-only BLEU is 0.347 versus 0.367, and extrinsic-only BLEU is 0.351 versus 0.369. Revised baseline and judge prompts are also not reconciled with unchanged benchmark results. These unresolved reporting problems make the net quality effect of the added evidence uncertain.
